title: Shortbread
subtitle: Classic Scottish butter shortbread
excerpt: The classic Scottish biscuit made with only three ingredients: butter, flour, and sugar. Pressed into a tin or cut into fingers and baked low and slow until pale golden and crumbly.

recipe.sourceNotes: Shortbread is the oldest and most austere of Scottish biscuits, with records of it appearing in sixteenth-century Scotland. Mary Queen of Scots is said to have been particularly fond of it. The original shortbread contained oatmeal and was a luxury reserved for special occasions such as Christmas and New Year (Hogmanay), when the round shortbread was associated with the sun and good fortune. As white flour became cheaper, oatmeal was gradually replaced. The traditional ratio is one part caster sugar, two parts butter, three parts flour, often written 1:2:3. The three most common forms are rounds or petticoat tails (a large circle marked into wedges), fingers (a rectangle cut into bars), and individual rounds stamped with a biscuit cutter.

recipeTools.notes: A 20 cm square baking tin or a flat baking tray.

content.text: The butter must be soft but not melted: this is the single most important variable. Cold butter will not combine smoothly; melted butter will produce a greasy, crumbling dough. Beat the butter and sugar before adding the flour, and handle the dough as little as possible once the flour is added: overworking develops gluten and makes the shortbread tough rather than sandy. Bake at a low temperature; the shortbread should be pale, not browned.
Heat the oven to 160 C / fan 140 C / gas 3. Beat the soft butter and caster sugar in a large bowl until pale and fluffy, about 3 minutes with a wooden spoon or electric beaters.

Add the flour and salt. Work together with your hands or a wooden spoon until the dough just comes together. Press into a 20 cm square tin or shape into fingers on a baking tray, about 1 cm thick. Prick all over with a fork.

Bake for 28 to 35 minutes until very pale golden but not browned. Dust with caster sugar immediately. If pressing into a tin, score into fingers while warm and leave to cool completely in the tin before removing. They will firm up as they cool.
